variants.intertext: The first tablet from Tell Harmal, IM 52615, contains an account of the portentous dreams that Gilgameš experienced on the journey to the Cedar Forest. The text is entirely direct speech: the first line of the tablet, which represents two lines of poetry, contains Enkidu’s instructions to Gilgameš for him to go up to the highest part of the mountain and look around. Lines 2–9, spoken by Gilgameš, report how the speaker, suddenly woken from sleep, related a dream he had been experiencing. The remaining text (ll. 10–17), in which someone explains the nightmare, is spoken by Enkidu:

%n kī laptat | kī nemiat | kī dalhat
#note: See @bib{RN117@250}: “The emendation of the second verb follows von Soden. The word @i{ne-ma-at} defies obvious interpretation as it stands. Alongside the etymology put forward by von Soden (@i{apû}, ‘to become dim’), one thinks also of @i{nawiʾat}, ‘it was a desolation’ (on @i{naw}/@i{mûm} see the commentary on @i{nu-ma-at} in OB III 108).”

manuscripts.atf: ki la-<ap?>-ta#-at# ki ne-ma-at# ki# da#-al#-ha-at

lines.translation: #tr.en: how ominous it was, how @i{desolate}, how confused!

variants.reconstruction:
%n anāku | rīmī (|) ṣērim | aṣṣabtānim
#note: See @bib{RN117@250}: “The remarkable plural ventive ending on the singular @i{aṣṣabtānim} elicited from von Soden another OB example, @akk{ki ta-da-am-mi-qu₂-nim} in the poem often called ‘Man and his God’ (@bib{nougayrol1952version@246}, re-edited by @bib{RN1657@192, 57}, who translates ‘that you are well favoured’). Von Soden’s hope that a larger number of examples would eventually elucidate the usage has not yet been fulfilled. T. Jacobsen put forward an ingenious explanation in his discussion of the ‘ablative accusative’, analysing -@i{nim} instead as ‘departive’ -@i{n}- and ‘the expected, but hitherto missing, first singular common dative pronominal suffix -@i{im}, “for me”’ (@bib{jacobsen1963akkadian@26}). It remains a virtuoso position, unsubstantiated by further enquiry, though B. R. Foster also views the ending as expressing the first-person reflexive (@bib{RN163@41, fn. 42}: ‘I captured for myself’). Tournay and Shaffer’s emendation to first-person pl. @i{niṣṣabtānim} (@bib{RN580@109, fn. 11}) does not make parsing the suffix any easier. In our present state of knowledge these are desperate remedies and it seems wise to resort to neither of them. Thus I ignore the ending and keep to von Soden’s ‘ich packte gerade’.”

Lambert, personal communication).”

ši-ip-r[a]-am ša la i-ba-aš-šu-<u₂> i-n[a] <ma>-tim

#note: @bib{RN117@251}: “On the penultimate sign see van Dijk, @i{TIM} IX, p. xi: ‘MA or MU impossible, hardly NA, most likely BE or NU, but NA is not excluded’. The emendations given here are confirmed by the appearance of the same line in the Yale tablet (OB III 17): @i{šipram ša lā ibaššû ina mātim}; cf. already @bib{RN2652@116, fn. 68}. The lack of @i{plene} marking of the final -@i{û} in this tablet may alternatively be explained as signifying a running together of @i{ibaššû} and @i{ina} (Lambert). Note the comparable spelling @akk{iṭ-hu-a-na} (OB Schøyen₂ 26) for @i{iṭḫû ana}.”
